The mainland hub a couple km away with parking, hotels, and the free shuttle bus or footbridge walk to the mount.

The nearest proper town, about 9 km south on the Couesnon, with the area's railway station (Pontorson-Mont-Saint-Michel), shops, supermarkets and the cheapest beds within reach of the Mont. It suits travellers arriving by train or watching the budget rather than anyone wanting the abbey on the doorstep.

landmarks: Abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel
The Gothic abbey church and its dizzying crypts crown the tidal island's granite summit, a UNESCO marvel of medieval engineering rising 80 meters above the bay.
La Merveille (Abbey Cloister and Refectory)
The 13th-century 'Marvel' stacks a serene columned cloister, luminous refectory, and knights' hall in three breathtaking Gothic storeys above the sea.
Grande Rue
The island's single medieval main street corkscrews upward past half-timbered houses, crêperies, and souvenir shops that have served pilgrims since the Middle Ages.
The Ramparts Walk
A circuit of 15th-century defensive walls and towers built during the Hundred Years' War delivers ever-changing panoramas over the vast tidal flats.
The Bay of Mont-Saint-Michel
Europe's most dramatic tides race across shimmering sands here; guided barefoot crossings of the bay are an unforgettable way to approach the Mount.
Église Saint-Pierre
The islanders' tiny parish church shelters a silver-clad statue of Saint Michael slaying the dragon, glowing with candles lit by pilgrims.
Chapelle Saint-Aubert
A humble stone chapel clinging to the rocks at the island's foot honors the bishop whose vision of the Archangel founded the Mount in 708.
Tour Gabriel
This stout 1524 artillery bastion guarding the western ramparts once carried a windmill and remains one of the island's most photographed fortifications.
Logis Tiphaine
The 14th-century house that knight Bertrand du Guesclin built for his scholarly wife Tiphaine offers a furnished glimpse of medieval island life.
Passerelle and Causeway Viewpoints
The elegant 2014 footbridge and the dam viewpoints on the mainland frame the classic postcard silhouette of the Mount mirrored in wet sand.

train.note: There is no station at Mont-Saint-Michel itself. The nearest railhead is Pontorson-Mont-Saint-Michel, 9 km away on the Caen-Rennes line, from which a connecting bus runs to the shuttle car park; Rennes, Dol-de-Bretagne and Villedieu-les-Poeles are the other usual approaches, all with TGV links to Paris Montparnasse in around 2-3 hours. SNCF Connect sells combined train-plus-coach tickets to Le Mont-Saint-Michel, which is the simplest way to book. No international train comes anywhere near - for the UK or Belgium you change in Paris or Rennes. Services are sparse on Sundays and out of season, so check the last connection back before you set out.

bus.note: No international coach serves Mont-Saint-Michel. Getting there means a regional coach: Keolis Armor runs the connecting services from Rennes, Pontorson and Dol-de-Bretagne timed to trains, and tickets are sold through SNCF Connect (https://www.sncf-connect.com/en-en/) or on board. From the visitor centre and car park at La Caserne, 2.5 km from the Mount, the free Le Passeur shuttle runs continuously to the causeway, or you can walk it in about 35 minutes. Day-trip coaches from Paris, Saint-Malo and Bayeux are also common and must be booked ahead in summer. See https://www.ot-montsaintmichel.com/en/ for current timetables.

ferry.note: Mont-Saint-Michel sits in a tidal bay with dangerous quicksand and huge tidal ranges, and has no harbour or scheduled boat service - access is on foot or by shuttle across the causeway. Guided walks across the bay sands are the only way to arrive by water, and must be done with a licensed guide. The nearest passenger ferries are at Granville, about 50 km north, where Manche Iles Express sails to Jersey, Guernsey and Sark (https://www.manche-iles.com/), and at Saint-Malo, an hour west, for Brittany Ferries' crossings to Portsmouth and the Channel Islands (https://www.brittany-ferries.co.uk/).

half.name: Saint-Malo
half.blurb: A walled Breton port city about an hour west, with granite ramparts encircling a historic old town on the English Channel.

half.name: Dinan
half.blurb: A medieval Breton hilltown about an hour west with half-timbered houses and a cobbled port on the Rance River.

half.name: Avranches
half.blurb: A Norman hilltop town about twenty minutes east with views back across the bay and a museum of illuminated manuscripts.

half.name: Bayeux
half.blurb: A Normandy town about ninety minutes northeast, home to the 70-meter Bayeux Tapestry depicting the 1066 Norman Conquest.
